reference_summary: – The Supreme Court is facing a docket of high-profile political cases that will test whether recent liberal victories were more fluke or firm conviction, the New York Times reports. The court—which is divided 5-4 for conservatives, but saw Justice Roberts vote liberal on Obamacare and same-sex marriage—will look at cases including unions, affirmative action, and possibly abortion. A primer: Unions: Since 1977, unions have been allowed to charge non-union workers for dues that go to collective bargaining efforts, but not political ones. Now California teachers have brought a case saying collective bargaining is itself political. "It could set the stage for a Citizens United-style reconsideration in the area of union dues," a lawyer says. Affirmative Action: Abigail Fisher says that being white played a role in the University of Texas denying her admission back in 2008. The Supreme Court punted on her case in 2013, and now it's back on the docket. Like the unions case, this was brought by a conservative group that recruited the plaintiffs. The death penalty: Justices will decide on capital-punishment cases in Pennsylvania, Kansas, Georgia, and Florida, the Wall Street Journal reports. Justices Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Stephen Breyer have already expressed doubts about whether capital punishment is constitutional. "One person, one vote": Should state legislative districts be drawn based on their number of people or eligible voters? If justices choose the latter—leaving out immigrants and children—Latinos could lose political clout and rural areas will gain, Politico reports. Abortion: Justices may opt to revisit a Texas law that could reduce the state's abortion clinics from more than 40 to roughly 10. At issue is whether new clinic requirements are an "undue burden" on women's right to an abortion. One commentator believes this Supreme Court session will be ugly for liberals.

issues.description: The graph re‑uses the same entity IDs for completely different people or concepts (e.g., entity_1 is both Rebecca Friedrichs and Vikram D. Amar). IDs must be unique; otherwise every relation that references these IDs is ambiguous and likely incorrect.

Relation "entity_5 –[ANNOUNCED]-> entity_19" claims that the source (Governor Walker) announced doubts about the death penalty, but the evidence quote is about Justices Breyer and Ginsburg. The source does not match the evidence.
Relation "entity_16 –[ANNOUNCED]-> entity_19" attributes the announcement about the death penalty to Jennifer Haberkorn, yet the cited quote never mentions her. She only contributed to the report.

This relation links the source (Rebecca Friedrichs) to the target (Catherine Fisk) with a LOCATED_IN label, but the supporting quote discusses the death‑penalty issue in Washington and has no geographical connection between the two persons.

The PARTICIPATED_IN relation between Rebecca Friedrichs and the case Friedrichs v. California Teachers Association includes an irrelevant quote about the term beginning on Monday, which does not support the participation claim.
The RELATED_TO edge from Justice Kennedy to the Abood case uses a quote about Justice Alito, not Kennedy. The evidence does not substantiate the claimed relationship.

Because of the duplicated IDs, the same ID is simultaneously used for a judge (e.g., entity_5) and a legal concept (capital sentences). This creates contradictory type assignments (PERSON vs. CONCEPT) within the same graph.

The entity "capital sentences" is typed as CONCEPT, yet it is used as the source of LOCATED_IN relations to states (Florida, Georgia, etc.). While not illegal, the relation type is more appropriate for a CASE or EVENT rather than a CONCEPT, indicating a mismatch between entity type and relation semantics.

grader_reports.feedback_summary: The extracted graph suffers from severe identifier collisions—many entities share the same ID despite representing different people or concepts—which renders most relations ambiguous or incorrect. Several relations are outright hallucinations, linking the wrong source to a target with unrelated evidence (e.g., announcements about the death penalty). A few edges contain weak or mismatched evidence, and duplicate IDs also cause type contradictions. To fix the graph, assign unique IDs to each distinct entity, verify that every relation’s source, target, and type are directly supported by the quoted text, and remove or correct any relations that are not substantiated.
